### Part 1 --- The question, the team, and the writing

Turn an interest into a question that can actually be answered, learn to write the problem down, and build a team that will still be functional in November.

|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | Aug 26 | **Where questions come from**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> The capstone arc into AEM 6992, and what this is not: you are not writing a paper for a journal, you are building the analysis a competent team needs before a decision that costs real money. Five project archetypes — evaluation, preference and pricing, prediction and risk, diagnosis and benchmarking, feasibility and landscape — with what each can claim, what design it needs, and how each fails. The anti-patterns, and the four-question feasibility filter. ### Part 2 --- Evidence, models, and inference

The conceptual core. What a causal claim is, what the standard models estimate, where uncertainty comes from, the difference between explaining and predicting, and how inference goes wrong. Taught on examples from industry and the news, before anyone opens a dataset.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 3 | Sep 9 | **Causal language**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Counterfactuals and potential outcomes; why every comparison is a claim about a world that did not happen. Causal graphs: confounders, colliders, mediators, back-door reasoning — and why controlling for everything makes things worse<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Draw the graph for your own project. Then Writing 1 is peer-swapped and critiqued in class — you will read somebody else's problem statement before you read your own again | Writing 1 — problem statement |
| 4 | Sep 16 | **Models, uncertainty, and prediction**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Linear regression, non-linear models, and count models — described, not derived: what each estimates and how to read a coefficient in the units of the problem. Then where uncertainty comes from: residuals and errors, sampling variation, what a standard error states, where p-values come from and what they are not. Finally the distinction that decides half the projects in this room — explaining versus predicting, and why a model that predicts well may tell you nothing about what to do<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Simulation lab: draw from a world you control. Watch the p-value distribution under the null, then change the sample size and the variation and watch it move. Then fit the same world in-sample and out-of-sample, and watch a model that looks excellent fail on data it has not seen. Nothing to install, no code to write | — |
| 5 | Sep 23\* | **How inference goes wrong**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Bias: omitted variables, sorting and selection, measurement error (classical and not), reverse causality — what each does to the estimate and in which direction. False precision: dependence ignored, multiple testing, specification search<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Take a published claim apart in breakouts: which failure is doing the damage, and would more data fix it? | — |
| 6 | Sep 30 | **Conditioning on what you can observe**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> What it means to identify an effect by conditioning on observables: controls, matching, and when a regression coefficient can be read causally. Why 'I added controls' is a claim about the graph rather than a technique, and exactly what would have to be true for it to hold<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Milestone 1: each team presents its research problem in five minutes and takes questions from the room. Then the first peer evaluation | Research problem presentation, in class · Peer evaluation 1 · Problem statement & literature review, end of week |

### Part 3 --- Research designs

The ways applied economists get a credible estimate, from conditioning on observables to designs built on found variation — what variation each exploits, what each assumes, and how each fails.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 7 | Oct 7 | **Research designs I**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Experiments; instrumental variables; regression discontinuity. What variation each exploits, what each assumes, how each fails, and what it looks like when it is done well<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Scenario clinic: given a question, would any of these three work here? | — |
| 8 | Oct 14 | **Research designs II**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Difference-in-differences; panel data with local fixed effects; event studies. What identifying variation survives once the fixed effects are in, and what assumption you are leaning on<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Name your own project's design, and the assumption you would have to defend | — |

### Part 4 --- Measurement, data, and getting hold of it

The step most projects skip. Turning a construct into something a dataset can hold, working out what the design actually demands, and then the practical business of obtaining it — sources, proprietary access, data-use agreements, the IRB, and what scraping and APIs can and cannot get you.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 9 | Oct 21\* | **Measurement, and what the design demands**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Constructs and operationalization: how you turn 'sustainability', 'financial literacy', or 'market power' into a variable somebody could actually record, and what makes that measure defensible or indefensible. Validity, and what a proxy costs you. Then working backwards from the design to its data requirements: unit of observation, level of aggregation, time frequency, span, coverage, and which comparisons the data has to contain — can this be done with county-level data, or does it need individuals?<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> What to ask of a dataset before trusting anything it says: what is one row? how many are there? what is missing, and is it missing at random? what is the range, and are the extremes real? what changed over time, and did the definition change with it? Then the measurement clinic — the variable your question actually needs, and whether anything on earth measures it | Writing 2 — limitation paragraph |
| 10 | Oct 28 | **Getting hold of the data**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> The landscape: administrative records, official statistics, firm and platform data, purchased panels — what each costs in money and in months. Proprietary access and data-use agreements: who signs, how long it takes, and what they forbid you from publishing. Research ethics and the Cornell IRB: what needs approval, what does not, and how long it takes. Then scraping and APIs at awareness level — what they are, what they can and cannot get you, what the terms of service and the law actually say, and when paying for a licence is the cheaper answer. We do not write scrapers in this course; you need to know what to ask for and what it costs<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Academic writing II — the memo. Writing to a decision-maker rather than an examiner: the two-page discipline, the bottom line first, and the fallback that shows you thought about failure. Then the acquisition clinic: each team names its source, its access route, its timeline, and its plan B | Data feasibility memo assigned |
| 11 | Nov 4 | **Midterm; interrogating data with an assistant**<br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> **Midterm** — you are given a situation and asked to design a study to evaluate it, in writing: the question, the design, what data it requires, and what would undermine it<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Real data in front of you, and the checklist from meeting 9 put to work through an assistant: summaries, joins, quick plots. Then the harder half — knowing whether the answer is right without reading the code. Row counts across a join, totals against a published figure, five raw records read by hand. What not to upload, and why | Data feasibility memo, end of week |

Seeing what a figure shows and hides, writing the design paper, keeping a team and a project functional, and the proposal that carries into AEM 6992.
